title: American Express Profit Jumps 28%, Raises Outlook, Cuts 3,500 Jobs
excerpt: Affluent customers kept the $895 Platinum Card and spent through the quarter, lifting revenue to a record $20.1 billion — while AmEx booked a $336 million charge to trim 5% of its workforce.
body:
• American Express third-quarter net income rose 28% to $3.71 billion; adjusted earnings of $4.68 per share beat the roughly $4.48 Wall Street consensus.
  • Revenue hit a record $20.1 billion, up 9%, as billed business rose 8% to $454 billion and affluent customers kept the refreshed $895 Platinum Card.
  • AmEx raised full-year guidance to $18.30-$18.60 reported and $17.60-$17.90 adjusted per share, and will cut about 3,500 jobs — roughly 5% of its workforce — booking a $336 million restructuring charge.
  • For cardholders, the test of the $200 Platinum fee increase is passing so far: nearly all members moved to the higher fee have kept the card, and net card fees rose by more than $400 million year on year.

American Express reported a sharp rise in third-quarter profit on Friday as affluent customers kept spending and accepted a higher-fee Platinum Card, and used the strength to raise its full-year outlook while announcing its first major job cuts in roughly a decade.

The New York-based company posted net income of $3.71 billion, up 28% from a year earlier, or $5.42 per share on a reported basis, according to the Associated Press. Excluding a one-time gain from the sale of its stake in Global Business Travel Group, adjusted earnings were $4.68 per share, ahead of Wall Street expectations of about $4.48 compiled by LSEG, Reuters reported. Revenue net of interest expense climbed 9% to a record $20.1 billion.

Spending held up, led by travel

Billed business — total spending on AmEx-issued cards — rose 8% to $454 billion. Travel and entertainment spending grew 10% from a year earlier, led by a 13% jump in airline spending and a 9% rise in restaurant spending, Reuters reported. Chief Financial Officer Christophe Le Caillec told Reuters that part of the airline increase reflected higher average ticket prices as carriers raised fares. The average cardmember spent $6,735 in the quarter, up 5%, the AP reported, and the company acquired 3.1 million new cards, 76% of them on fee-paying products, according to its earnings call.

The Platinum refresh was the quarter's central commercial question. AmEx raised the card's annual fee last year from $695 to $895 while adding benefits. The company said nearly all customers transitioned to the higher fee have kept the card, and net card fees grew 17% on an FX-adjusted basis. Credit quality also improved: provisions for credit losses were about $1 billion, and the net write-off rate eased to 1.8% from 1.9%.

"We have got good momentum, but to accelerate innovation and win over the next few years, we needed to become a more agile and efficient organization."

— Stephen Squeri, Chairman and CEO, American Express

Outlook raised, 3,500 jobs to go

AmEx raised its full-year 2026 guidance to $18.30 to $18.60 per share on a reported basis, or $17.60 to $17.90 adjusted, lifting the low end of its previous $17.30 to $17.90 adjusted range, and reaffirmed 10% revenue growth. Full results are posted on the company's investor relations site.

Alongside the raise, Chief Executive Stephen Squeri told analysts the company will eliminate approximately 5% of its positions globally — about 3,500 employees — and recorded a $336 million restructuring charge in the quarter. Squeri said strong performance had enabled AmEx to step up marketing and technology investment, and that part of the gain from the Global Business Travel transaction was being used to make the organisation more efficient. He stressed the cuts were about speed and agility, not a downturn in business — a point the AP also reported. Shares slipped in morning trading despite the beat, extending a pattern analysts have noted of the stock falling on results day.

For investors, the quarter frames a clear trade: a premium customer base that has absorbed a $200 fee increase and kept spending, funding heavier rewards and marketing costs, with the restructuring intended to keep expenses from outrunning that growth into 2027.
